newsitem.title: USA: New England battered by severe late winter storm.
newsitem.headline: New England battered by severe late winter storm.

text.p: New England was battered by a severe blizzard on Monday with winds gusting up to 70 mph (110 kph) and snowfall predicted to reach 20 inches (50 cm) as winter refused to give way to spring in America's north-east.

A vicious northeaster plunged most of New England and upstate New York back into the depths of winter, and the day-long blizzard conditions were expected to last into Tuesday, according to the National Weather Service

"It's going to be the worst storm of the year," said Michael Dion, a National Weather Service spokesman in Taunton, Mass. "We have not seen real heavy, wet snow anywhere this winter. Also, this storm's going to be a real slow mover, which means it's going to be of a long duration.

"It's going to cause a lot of wind of up to 60 to 70 mph (96-110 kph), coastal flooding problems, and a lot of other problems. The worst of the storm, in terms of snow, will be overnight tonight," Dion said.
Boston's Logan International Airport reported delays of up to one hour on some flights, as several airlines reported cancelling their flights.
Many schools in the region closed early on Monday as the storm turned from heavy rain to sleet, to heavy, wet snow. A number of schools said they would remain closed on Tuesday.
New York State police reported dozens of traffic accidents due to the severe weather.
"Cars are all over the place and there are lots of accidents," Trooper Andrew Lindeman said. "The interstates are a mess and I am sure the back roads are too."
Visibility was expected to be less than a quarter-mile at times, with the wind creating drifting snow.
Utility companies from Connecticut and Rhode Island through Maine geared up for expected widespread outtages from downed power lines caused by the wet, heavy snow and high winds.
Boston Edison, Eastern Utilities, and Northeast Utilities all reported putting extra crews on standby to deal with the outtages.
Marine storm warnings were also in effect from Long Island to the Gulf of Maine as the weather service expected wind gusts to reach hurricane force at times off-shore.
"Anybody on a boat out there is going to get rocked tonight," National Weather Service forecaster Art Lester said by telephone from his office in Grey, Maine.
There may be a silver lining to the spring storm. Some ski areas are considering re-opening for as long as the new snow lasts. A number of resorts closed for the season during the past two weeks.
"We've had quite a few calls. We are hoping to open, even if only for a few days," said Michelle Merryman, manager of the Mt. Tom Ski Area in western Massachusetts.
